report.query: Compare multi-agent LLM frameworks for collaborative reasoning

per_paper_summaries.title: AgentVerse: Facilitating Multi-Agent Collaboration and Exploring Emergent Behaviors
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: AgentVerse introduces a framework for multi-agent collaboration that enhances performance on reasoning and coding tasks while exploring emergent cooperative and competitive behaviors.

per_paper_summaries.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: AutoGen presents a scalable multi-agent conversation framework that outperforms single-agent systems on diverse benchmarks.

per_paper_summaries.title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: The survey offers a unified framework for reviewing LLM-based autonomous agent research and highlights key open challenges in the field.

per_paper_summaries.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: AgentBench provides a benchmark for assessing LLMs as autonomous agents, revealing performance gaps in long-horizon tasks and the need for integrated evaluation of agent behavior.

per_paper_summaries.title: OpenAgents: An Open Platform for Language Agents in the Wild
per_paper_summaries.one_sentence_summary: OpenAgents delivers a comprehensive platform infrastructure for deploying LLM agents at scale, facilitating reproducible research and interaction log analysis.

overlaps.description: Both papers address the limitations of single-agent systems and the need for structured collaboration among multiple agents to achieve complex tasks.
Both papers propose frameworks involving structured collaboration among multiple agents to enhance task performance.
Both papers highlight the challenges in evaluating LLM-based agents, with a focus on the lack of standardized evaluation and the need for integrated assessment of agent behavior.

differences.title: AgentVerse: Facilitating Multi-Agent Collaboration and Exploring Emergent Behaviors
differences.description: The framework dynamically recruits expert agents and facilitates structured collaboration phases, focusing on emergent cooperative and competitive behaviors among agents.

differences.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
differences.description: The framework uses structured conversation among multiple LLM-powered agents, each with a defined role, to address complex reasoning and multi-step task execution.

differences.title: A Survey on Large Language Model based Autonomous Agents

differences.title: AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents

gaps.problem_formulation: Coordinating multiple agents toward a shared goal requires structured collaboration.
gaps.description: While the problem of coordinating multiple agents is addressed through a dynamic framework in AgentVerse, there is no mention of using benchmarking as a method to evaluate the effectiveness of such coordination strategies.
gaps.supporting_evidence: AgentVerse focuses on a framework for collaboration but does not mention any benchmarking method to evaluate coordination.

gaps.problem_formulation: Single-agent systems face fundamental limitations in complex reasoning and multi-step task execution.
gaps.description: AutoGen addresses the limitations of single-agent systems through multi-agent conversation but does not explore deploying these systems on an open platform for real-world application testing.
gaps.supporting_evidence: AutoGen uses structured conversation but lacks a method for deployment on an open platform as seen in OpenAgents.

gaps.problem_formulation: The lack of a unified conceptual framework for LLM-based autonomous agents and the identification of open challenges.
gaps.description: The survey identifies challenges and lacks a unified framework but does not propose a collaborative framework to address these challenges, unlike the structured collaboration in AgentVerse.
gaps.supporting_evidence: The survey identifies challenges but does not propose a collaborative framework as a method to address them.

gaps.problem_formulation: The rapid development of LLM-based agents lacks standardized evaluation.
gaps.description: AgentBench provides a benchmarking method but does not incorporate a collaborative framework to enhance the evaluation process of LLM-based agents.
gaps.supporting_evidence: AgentBench focuses on benchmarking but does not use a collaborative framework as a method.

gaps.problem_formulation: Most LLM agent research evaluates on benchmarks without production deployment infrastructure.
gaps.description: OpenAgents provides a platform for deployment but does not include a survey method to gather insights or challenges from the deployment of LLM agents in real-world settings.
gaps.supporting_evidence: OpenAgents focuses on deployment infrastructure but lacks a survey method to evaluate the deployment outcomes.

report.synthesis: The papers collectively illustrate the evolving landscape of multi-agent frameworks for collaborative reasoning using large language models (LLMs). AgentVerse and AutoGen both demonstrate the effectiveness of structured collaboration among multiple agents, addressing the limitations of single-agent systems in complex tasks. Meanwhile, AgentBench and the survey by Lei Wang et al. emphasize the challenges in evaluating LLM-based agents, noting the absence of standardized evaluation methods and the need for a unified conceptual framework. OpenAgents contributes by providing the infrastructure for real-world deployment, yet there remains a gap in integrating benchmarking and open platform deployment to evaluate collaborative strategies effectively. Overall, while significant strides have been made in multi-agent LLM frameworks, a consistent approach to evaluation and deployment in real-world scenarios is still needed.
